title: Raga Kedara

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Tukhari, and your line was Nanak's months. What was this month's weather carrying when you looked out? Day one thousand one hundred ten.

Evening has its own sound. Dishes clinking. A door closing down the hall. The day's conversations still replaying: who praised you, who didn't, what someone said that stung. Right about then, as the house goes quiet, tradition sets a raga down gently: Kedara, a short section of the Guru Granth Sahib this path calls tender, for the evening. And inside it is a hymn that speaks straight to those replaying conversations. Today, Raga Kedara.
screen: `DISHES, A DOOR, THE DAY REPLAYING.` → `A TENDER RAGA FOR EVENING.` → `RAGA KEDARA.`

segments.voice: Kedara holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and after them, the voices of Bhagats: Kabir and Ravidas. Today, Kabir. Here's his hymn in Kedara, given in plain English, not word for word: set aside both praise and slander; give up pride and self-conceit. The one who looks on iron and gold alike, Kabir says, is an image of God. Here's how evening can go. The compliments get replayed and polished. The criticism gets replayed and argued with. Both keep the mind awake. Kabir asks for something quieter: let go of both. Not just the insult. The praise too. That's the tender part, and it's also the hard part. Setting down a compliment can feel like losing something. One way to read Kabir: both praise and blame tie a person to other people's opinions, and the mind can't rest while it's tied. Iron and gold alike isn't a rule against nice things. It's a picture of a mind that doesn't jump when the world calls it gold, and doesn't sink when the world calls it iron. A raga for evening is a good place for that hymn. The day's verdicts are in; the evening is when you can decide not to carry them to bed. Tradition gives Kedara a gentle color, and Kabir uses it to loosen the grip of the day. Tomorrow we'll listen to another Bhagat in this raga, at dusk. That's today's line: tender evening.
screen: `GURUS FIRST, THEN KABIR AND RAVIDAS.` · `SET ASIDE PRAISE AND SLANDER.` · `IRON AND GOLD ALIKE.` · `DON'T CARRY THE VERDICTS TO BED.` · then, large: `TENDER EVENING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set down the day's verdicts. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one piece of praise from today, or this week, and one piece of criticism. Hold one in each hand, if it helps to picture it: one gold, one iron. Notice which one is heavier. Then, on an out-breath, set them both down beside you, the praise and the blame, as if setting down two bags at the end of a long walk. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set them down. If you don't, simply let your hands rest open. Later today, listen to one Kedara shabad. The bell holds the time.
Raga Kedara. A short, tender evening raga where Kabir sings: set aside praise and slander, and look on iron and gold alike. Today's word.
Your line: tender evening. Tonight, before sleep, let go of one compliment and one criticism from today, both of them, on purpose. Day one thousand one hundred ten.

howItsDone: Shabads from the Kedara section, including the Bhagats' hymns by Kabir and Ravidas, are sung in Raga Kedara in kirtan, and tradition associates the raga with the evening.
